function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** that you can copy‑paste into a terminal (or run as a single shell script) to finish the whole workflow.  
I’ve also included the exact file contents that should be added to the repository.

> **⚠️ Important** – The helper functions you listed are only for generating a *Python* Dockerfile and a *generic* Kubernetes YAML.  
> Because the target repo is a **Node.js** application, I’ll hand‑craft the Dockerfile and the Kubernetes manifests instead of calling those functions.  
> If you still want to use the helper functions for the other parts, you can do so – they’re perfectly fine for the Kubernetes YAML and the GitHub Actions workflow.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use the official Node.js 18 slim image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD [ "node", "app.js" ]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and contains everything needed to run a Node.js app.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a clean install from `package-lock.json`.  
> * The app is assumed to listen on port **3000** – adjust if your app uses a different port.

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s-deployment.yaml` in the root of the repo with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: nodejs-welcome:latest   # Replace with your registry/tag if needed
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys 2 replicas of the container.  
> * Exposes the container’s port 3000 to the cluster via a `ClusterIP` service on port 80.  
> * Adjust `image:` to point to your container registry (e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`).

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout source
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest

      - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
        # Uncomment and configure if you have a K8s cluster set up
        # uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v3
        # with:
        #   manifests: k8s-deployment.yaml
        #   images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
```

> **What this workflow does**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Builds a Docker image from the repo’s `Dockerfile`.  
> * Pushes the image to GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`).  
> * (Optional) You can uncomment the deployment step if you have a K8s cluster configured in the repo’s secrets.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s-deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run, build the image, and push it to the registry.

---

## Optional: Verify everything

```bash
# Check the Docker image exists in GHCR
docker pull ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest

# Apply the Kubernetes manifests (if you have a cluster)
kubectl apply -f k8s-deployment.yaml
```

---

### Recap of the files created

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s-deployment.yaml` | Deploys the app to Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI pipeline that builds & pushes the image |

Feel free to tweak the image tags, registry, or Kubernetes settings to match your environment. Happy coding!
